messages.subject: parallel RNG & gradient testing
parts:
The gradient testing now happens after user
or random inits. And it also now prints out
the param values as well as the gradients.

I decided it'd be easier to just go ahead and
implement the parallel RNG stuff so I could
stop worrying about it. It'll also look better
in the paper.s

I just committed a version that uses parallel
random number generation a la L'Ecuyer. The
--help option on a compiled model gives you
the options, but the relevant ones here are:

--seed=<int>
--chain_id=<int>

So if you're running 4 parallel chains, give them
each different ids, starting from 1.

The period for L'Ecuyer is around 2**61. I back-of-the-enveloped
a skip-ahead (aka discard) of 2**50 (1 trillion) samples per chain,
allowing us 2**11 (2 thousand) distinct parallel chains.
So if they give us chain ID of 27, we skip ahead 27 * 2**50 samples
from the start of the chain with the given seed to start.

L'Ecuyer's method as implemented in Boost is about 8%
of the speed of the Mersenne Twister according to their
benchmarking, but it'd be easy enough to switch back or
even allow user specification of the random number generator.

Here's the original code for the Mersenne Twister:

// FASTER, but no parallel guarantees
// typedef boost::mt19937 rng_t;
// rng_t base_rng(static_cast<unsigned int>(random_seed
// + chain_id - 1));

typedef boost::ecuyer1988 rng_t;
rng_t base_rng(chain_random_seed);
// (2**50 = 1T samples, 1000 chains)
static boost::uintmax_t DISCARD_STRIDE = 1 << 50;
base_rng.discard(DISCARD_STRIDE * (chain_id - 1));

...

stan::mcmc::nuts<rng_t> sampler(model, delta, -1, base_rng);

There's no RNG base class with virtual methods, which is
why the code looks how it does with typedefs. This design's
faster because of no virtual functions, but a bit more of a pain
to plug and play -- if we want to allow the user to specify
which one they use, I'll need to template out a subroutine
based on the type of the RNG. It would have been convenient
had they gone with the curiously recurring template pattern
like Eigen does for matrices.

- Bob
